title: Welcome and Table of Contents
summary: What SS1 Christian Religious Studies Third Term covers (prayer, witnessing, persecution, impartiality, the Resurrection and Second Coming, God's sovereignty) and a map of every unit.

p: In this last term of SS1 you will study how to pray effectively, how to live as a witness for Christ in your school and nation, how to meet persecution, why God demands fairness, the hope of the Resurrection and the return of Jesus, and the sovereignty of God shown in creation. The topics link faith to everyday life: prayer, honesty, citizenship, courage and hope.

Read the Bible texts first, then the notes. Each unit has practice questions at the end. They do not count towards a mark; they help you to check your understanding. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit. Write the key verse of each unit in your notebook.

title: Effective Prayer
summary: What prayer is, James's teaching for different seasons, the conditions and hindrances of prayer, types of prayer (ACTS) and Elijah as an example.

p: Read James 1:5-8; 4:2-3; 5:13-18; Matthew 6:5-6. Prayer is close, personal communion with God. It is not just reciting words; it needs concentration and attention. We bring our will in line with God's will and, as Jesus taught, pray to the Father in His name. Effective prayer is prayer that gets results: it comes from someone who does not doubt that God is real, willing and able to answer.

If you lack wisdom, ask God in faith. If you are suffering, pray. If you are cheerful, sing praise. If you are sick, call the elders of the church to pray and anoint with oil. The prayer of faith will save the sick and the Lord will raise him up.

Conditions for success: faith (we must believe that God hears); right motive ('You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions'); righteousness and confession of sin; and humility and privacy, not praying to impress people.
Hindrances: doubt (a doubter is like a wave of the sea driven by the wind); cherished sin and unforgiveness; giving up too soon.

Adoration: praising God for who He is. Thanksgiving: thanking Him for what He has done. Confession: admitting sins and deciding to leave them. Petition: asking for our own needs. Intercession: standing in the gap for others, such as the sick or the nation. Dedication: promising to be God's own and to submit to His will. The memory aid ACTS stands for Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving and Supplication.

James says 'Elijah was a man with a nature like ours' (James 5:17), with feelings, fears and weaknesses. Yet he prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain for three and a half years; then he prayed again and the heavens gave rain. The power of prayer lies in the God who answers, and in a person who is right with Him.

title: Witnessing to Christ: A Holy Life among Others
summary: Witnessing as a lifestyle, Peter's call to holiness and good conduct among unbelievers, and Paul's call to wake up and put on Christ.

p: Read 1 Peter 1:13-17; 2:9-25; Romans 13:11-14. Witnessing is not only preaching. It is a life that is open, accountable and holy, a 'silent sermon' that others can see.

Prepare your mind ('gird up the loins of your mind'): be self-controlled and set your hope on the grace to come. Do not go back to your former desires and ignorance. Among non-believers keep your conduct honourable, so that even if they accuse you of doing wrong, they may see your good deeds and glorify God.
Peter's four commands: honour everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God, honour the king. Submit to every human authority for the Lord's sake.

Paul says the time is urgent: 'The night is far gone; the day is at hand.' Christians must wake from spiritual sleep. Throw off the works of darkness (drunkenness, immorality, quarrelling, jealousy) and 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ' like armour, making no provision for the flesh. The aim is to be a copy of Christ in society.
In school, witnessing means honesty in tests, respect for teachers and prefects, kindness to classmates and care for the school compound. Your life will speak before your words do.

title: Civic Responsibility, Social Vices and Peaceful Living
summary: Social vices that damage witness, tolerance and coexistence, why Christians obey government (Romans 13), and the duties of a good citizen.

p: Social vices are bad habits and tendencies in a community that work against peace and progress: drug abuse, bribery, corruption, stealing, armed robbery, sexual immorality, tribalism, nepotism and examination malpractice. A Christian who cheats in exams or takes bribes destroys his witness.

Tolerance means being fair and understanding towards people with different views, cultures, religions or races. Coexistence is living together without rancour. They build the nation and help the economy. Tolerance does not mean accepting sin; it means respecting the person while keeping your own faith.

Paul teaches that authority comes from God, and that rulers are God's servants for our good, to punish wrong and to reward good. So to resist lawful government is to resist what God has set up. In Peter's and Paul's day the ruler was the Roman emperor, who often persecuted Christians, so the call to respect leaders is strong.
But submission has limits: when the government commands something clearly against God's law, as in Daniel 3, believers must obey God first, peacefully and respectfully.

Pay taxes, rates and bills on time. Obey the law and road signs. Use freedom as a servant of God, not as a cover for evil. Keep away from crimes such as drug trafficking and cultism. A Christian lives in two kingdoms, God's kingdom and the state, and should be a model citizen in both.

title: Christian Attitudes towards Persecution
summary: What persecution is, Peter's picture of gold in the fire, rejoicing and hope, and James on the difference between trials and temptation.

p: Persecution is mistreating, threatening, harming or killing someone because of their religious beliefs. Christians may be hated because they stand against wrongs like fraud, corruption and cultism; their goodness shows up the darkness in others. Because it hurts, people are tempted to give in and tolerate evil.

sections.h: Peter: gold in the fire (1 Peter 1:6-9; 3:13-17; 4:12-19)
p: Faith is like gold, which is purified by fire. Persecution is the fire that burns away impurities such as hypocrisy and self-reliance, leaving a pure faith that gives praise to Jesus.

Do not be surprised at the fiery trial as if something strange were happening. Rejoice, because you share in Christ's sufferings and will share His glory. If you suffer as a murderer or thief, be ashamed; if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed. Suffering for doing wrong is not persecution. Set your hope on the grace to be given when Jesus returns.

'Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life.' James also corrects a mistake: God does not tempt anyone. God tests faith to strengthen it, but temptation comes from our own desire. The chain is: desire, then sin, then death.

It is not easy to live right among friends who do wrong. Prayer gives grace to stand. Persecution is not a sign that God is absent; it is a trial of faith. The Christian answer is joy, endurance and hope. Forms in school: being left out, mocking, and cyberbullying because of faith.

activity: Read 1 Peter 4:12-16. Write a short paragraph to encourage a friend who is bullied for going to church.

title: Impartiality
summary: What impartiality means, James's warning about favouring the rich, four reasons against partiality, the Golden Rule, and the harm of nepotism and tribalism.

p: Impartiality is acting without bias. It treats all people as equal brothers and sisters regardless of race, background or influence, and gives right judgment without fear or favour: looking at the facts, not the faces. All people are equal because God made each one in His own image, and He treats all generously.

sections.h: James 2:1-13: the rich man and the poor man
p: Two men come into the church. One wears gold rings and fine clothes; the other is poor and dressed in rags. The usher tells the rich man 'Have a seat here, please' and tells the poor man 'Stand there' or 'Sit at my feet'. James says, 'Have you not made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?'

Four reasons against partiality: God has chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom; the rich often oppress believers and drag them to court; favouritism breaks the 'royal law', 'You shall love your neighbour as yourself'; and God Himself is not partial.
Jesus taught in Matthew 7:12 and Luke 6:31: 'Whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them.' Before you act, ask: 'If I were in his place, how would I want to be treated?'

Nepotism is giving jobs and favours to relatives. Favouritism is treating some people better out of feeling. Tribalism is loyalty to your tribe together with hostility to others. These vices slow development, because wealth and power are shared unfairly. They also divide people, cause distrust and strife, and kill patriotism as people serve their clan, not the nation.
Loving your family is good, but when it twists justice it becomes sin. Choosing people by merit (their ability) is more in line with impartiality than choosing by connection.

title: The Resurrection of Jesus Christ
summary: What the Resurrection is and why it is the hub of the Christian faith, Matthew's account, and the role of the women.

p: Read Matthew 28:1-8 and Mark 16:1-8. The Resurrection means that Jesus rose from the dead on the third day after His crucifixion. It is the hub, the centre, of the Christian faith: without it the faith is empty (1 Corinthians 15:17). It confirms that Jesus is the Son of God and has power over sin and death. It also fulfils prophecy that God's Holy One would not see corruption (Psalm 16:10), and it shows that life continues beyond the grave.

On the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to the tomb. There was a great earthquake as an angel of the Lord came down, rolled back the stone and sat on it. His appearance was like lightning. The guards shook with fear and became like dead men. The angel told the women, 'Do not be afraid. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said.' They were told to go quickly and tell the disciples to meet Jesus in Galilee.

In a world where a woman's word counted for little, the Gospels name women as the first witnesses. They stayed near Jesus when most of the male disciples ran away. They went early to anoint His body, using spices they bought. Their love and courage were rewarded by being first to hear the news. If the disciples were inventing a story, they would not have chosen women as the first witnesses, which supports the truth of the accounts.
Lazarus was brought back to life but died again. This is resuscitation. Jesus rose to eternal life, and He is the first of many who will rise (1 Corinthians 15:20).

title: The Second Coming of Jesus Christ
summary: What the Second Coming and the Rapture mean, the signs Paul gives (rebellion and the man of lawlessness), and how Christians should prepare and comfort one another.

p: Read 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 and 2 Thessalonians 2:1-12. The Second Coming (Parousia) means that Jesus Christ will return. The notes teach that He will take faithful Christians to be with Him, which is often called the Rapture, and it is the believer's 'blessed hope'. No one knows the day or hour. He will come suddenly, 'like a thief in the night'.

Paul warns the Thessalonians not to be deceived by rumours that the day has already come. First, a great rebellion or falling away from the faith must happen. The 'man of lawlessness' will be revealed. He will exalt himself above God and use false miracles with Satan's power. God sends a strong delusion on those who refused to love the truth. The Lord Jesus will overthrow him 'with the breath of his mouth' and the brightness of His coming. Christians hold different views about how and when these things happen, but all agree that we must stay faithful.

Live holy lives as children of light. Show love and hospitality (Matthew 25). Share the Gospel to save others. Because the time is unknown, we must always be ready. This should affect even hidden sins: He comes like a thief.

Paul wrote about this to comfort Christians who had lost loved ones. For a believer, death is like sleep, a passing to be with Christ. The dead in Christ will rise first; then those alive will be caught up with them in the clouds to meet the Lord. 'Therefore encourage one another with these words.'

title: The Sovereignty of God
summary: What sovereignty means, the first account of creation (six days of order), the second account (God close to man), and how the two fit together.

p: Sovereign means holding the highest power without limit. God's sovereignty is His supremacy over all things. He is the supreme commander and controller who made everything. He gave man dominion over the earth (Genesis 1:28), but God's power is above man's. Man is a steward; God is the owner.
God brings order out of chaos ('without form and void'). By His word:

head: Day
What God made
rows: The sky (firmament), dividing waters above and below
Land and sea; plants and trees
Land animals and man in God's image
God rested, blessed the day and made it holy

p: This account looks closely at man and his home. There was no rain yet and no one to farm, so a mist watered the ground. God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, so man became a living being: a close, personal Creator. God planted the Garden of Eden with trees for beauty and food. Four rivers flowed from Eden: Pishon, Gihon, Tigris and Euphrates. God caused a deep sleep to fall on Adam, took one of his ribs, and made woman to be a suitable helper.

The two accounts do not contradict each other. They give two views: the wide view of God's power over the universe (Genesis 1, 'Elohim', God of power) and the close view of God's care for people (Genesis 2, 'Yahweh', God of relationship). God's 'rest' on the seventh day does not mean that He was tired; it means that the work was complete.
Because God is sovereign, we are accountable to Him. He is the owner; we are tenants and stewards of what He has made.
